name: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome

criteria.description: Clinical evidence of neurovascular compression in the thoracic outlet region
Positive provocative maneuvers such as Adson's, Roos, or Wright's test reproducing symptoms
Imaging evidence (e.g., MRI, CT angiography) demonstrating compression of neurovascular structures
Electrodiagnostic studies showing nerve conduction abnormalities consistent with brachial plexus involvement

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of clinical neurovascular compression symptoms plus at least one positive provocative maneuver; imaging and electrodiagnostic studies supportive but not mandatory
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging and electrodiagnostic studies aid in confirmation and exclusion of other causes

imaging: MRI or CT angiography showing compression of subclavian vessels or brachial plexus
Doppler ultrasound demonstrating altered blood flow in subclavian artery or vein
other: Electrodiagnostic studies showing nerve conduction delay or axonal loss in brachial plexus distribution
Positive provocative maneuvers (Adson's, Roos, Wright's tests)

distinguishingFeatures: Pain and neurological symptoms follow a dermatomal pattern
Symptoms localized to median nerve distribution in the hand
Positive Tinel's and Phalen's tests at the wrist
No vascular symptoms or supraclavicular findings

redFlags: Sudden onset of severe upper limb swelling and cyanosis
Signs of arterial ischemia such as pallor, coldness, or absent pulses
references: Illig KA, et al. Thoracic outlet syndrome: clinical review and current concepts. J Vasc Surg. 2010.
Peek J, et al. Diagnosis and management of thoracic outlet syndrome. J Hand Surg Am. 2018.
